title: Pride in success
tomorrow: Simran's Nitnem streak is long now. is that pride too?

cards: The email comes on a Thursday: Simran got into the college she wanted. She screams, Maya screams back over the phone, and her dad pretends he isn't crying. Simran calls Bebe and reads it out.
Bebe says congratulations, putt, and then something strange: and who did you thank? Simran laughs. Thank?
I wrote the essays! Bebe hums. Then she says: ten things, one thing.
Look it up. It's in the Sukhmani. Simran finds the passage that night, reads it twice, and still doesn't get it.

teach.h: ANG 268: TEN THINGS, ONE HELD BACK.
teach.b: Here's the puzzle, on ang 268, in paraphrase. Someone is given ten things and puts them behind him. Then one thing is held back, and over that one, he loses his trust.
If the giver held back that one and took the ten as well, the passage asks, what could the fool say?
The answer: because ten gifts stop feeling like gifts so fast. They start feeling earned, then owed. That's ahankar, pride, the fifth thief on ang 600.
It steals the thank-you, and without the thank-you, the next good thing feels owed too. Simran did write the essays, and Gurbani doesn't erase effort; honest work is part of the Sikh way.
But the mind that wrote them, the teacher who read the versions, the dad who drove the night routes, the quiet mornings she happened to be well: none of those were things she made.
The same passage gives the cure, in paraphrase: place the thing before the One it belongs to. Here's the line worth repeating: a trophy says look what I did; a gift says look what I was given.

The next morning Simran calls Bebe back and lists everyone, out loud: her English teacher, the counselor, her dad, Bhua Kiran, Maya, even the friend who quizzed her before every test. It takes a while.

how: Many Sikhs mark good news with thanks: an Ardas of gratitude at the gurdwara or at home, sometimes with karah prashad shared afterward.

o: being glad you worked hard and it paid off
forgetting the gifts inside your own success
wanting a prize that someone else deserves

games.q: ten things, one thing — tap the pairs.
p: ten things given, one held back

s: Sikh teaching says your own effort doesn't count
Gurbani doesn't erase effort; honest work is part of the Sikh way. pride steals the thank-you, not the work.
the Sukhmani tells of someone who forgets ten gifts over one held back
ang 268: and the cure is to place the thing before the One it belongs to.
humility means saying your success was all luck
the lesson isn't to deny the work, but to see the gifts inside it and thank the giver.

games.q: you get the promotion. at dinner, a cousin says, you earned every bit of it. what fits today's line?
o: thank them, and name the people who helped you get there.
agree: you earned it, and false modesty is dishonest.
insist it was luck, so nobody thinks you're proud.
games.why: a gift says look what i was given. the work was real; so were the teachers, the rides and the mornings you happened to be well.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that went well for you lately, big or small. Then count, finger by finger, the people and gifts that made it possible: a teacher, a ride, a good night's sleep, a voice that said keep going.
Go past the first few, and breathe with the count.

wordCard.voice: Pride in success. Ahankar, the thief that turns gifts into trophies and steals the thank-you.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ahankar, pride or ego, the fifth of the five thieves named on ang 600.

carryVoice: Gifts, not trophies: ten things given, and a giver to remember behind them. Congratulations, Simran.

sources.ref: Ang 268 (Gauri Sukhmani, Mahala 5, ashtpadi 5: das bastoo lai paachhai paavai, ek bast kaaran bikhott gavaavai … jis kee bast tis aagai raakhai), paraphrased
Ang 600 (Sorath, Mahala 3: the five thieves, ending with ahankaar), paraphrased
